subject: English
name: English, Units 1 and 2
about: VCE, Reading, crafting texts and argument
syllabus: VCE English and EAL Study Design (from 2023), Units 1 and 2

points.title: Making a personal response
points.brief: A personal response connects a text to your own experience and views, while still pointing to what the text shows.

points.title: Reading for inference
points.brief: Good readers work out what a text suggests but does not say, from hints in word choice, detail and what is left out.

points.title: Ideas, concerns and tensions
points.brief: A text explores ideas and concerns, such as belonging or power, and tensions between people or values drive it.

points.title: The world of a text
points.brief: Each text builds its own world of places, people, time and values, which readers enter as they read.

points.title: Characters and their choices
points.brief: Writers show character through actions, speech, thoughts and how others react, and choices reveal what a character values.

points.title: Point of view and narration
points.brief: First-person narration gives one view from inside; third-person can range across many minds. The choice shapes what readers know.

points.title: Structure and how a text unfolds
points.brief: Order of events, flashbacks, shifts in time and where a text starts and ends all shape meaning and suspense.

points.title: Writing about a text
points.brief: A good response makes a clear claim, supports it with short, well-chosen evidence and explains how the evidence shows it.

points.title: Purpose, audience and context
points.brief: Every piece of writing is shaped by why it is written, who will read it and the situation it is written in.

points.title: Generating ideas
points.brief: Brainstorming, freewriting, borrowing a first line or starting from an image are ways to find and grow an idea for writing.

points.title: Mentor texts
points.brief: Studying published texts as models to learn techniques, such as how an opening hooks a reader, then trying them in your own writing.

points.title: Text types and forms
points.brief: Forms such as short stories, personal essays, speeches, podcasts, poems and feature articles each have conventions readers expect.

points.title: Language modes
points.brief: Writing for the page, for speaking aloud or for a screen changes how a piece is structured and how it makes meaning.

points.title: Language choices for effect
points.brief: Word choice, imagery, sentence length and tone are chosen to create a mood or reaction in the reader.

points.title: Voice
points.brief: The personality a reader hears in a piece of writing, shaped by word choice, tone and rhythm.

points.title: Drafting and refining
points.brief: Writers draft, get feedback, revise structure and polish language, and can explain why each change was made.

points.title: Reflecting on your choices
points.brief: Writers explain the choices they made in a piece, and how each serves its purpose and audience.

units.title: Unit 2: Reading texts and exploring argument

chapters.title: Reading and exploring a second text

points.title: Analysing how a text is built
points.brief: Analytical responses look at how a writer's choices of language, structure and form create meaning, not only what happens.

points.title: Values in a text
points.brief: Texts show values, such as loyalty or justice, that characters hold or that the writer seems to support or question.

points.title: Context and a text
points.brief: The historical context of a text, and the social and cultural values in it, shape its ideas and how readers respond.

points.title: Building an analytical paragraph
points.brief: A topic sentence makes a claim, evidence supports it, analysis explains it, and a link ties it back to the question.

points.title: Using quotations well
points.brief: Short quotations woven into your own sentences show close reading better than long quotations.

points.title: Issues in the media
points.brief: An issue is a topic people disagree on, debated in news, opinion pieces, speeches, podcasts and social media.

points.title: Contention
points.brief: The contention is the main point a writer argues, the position they want readers to accept.

points.title: Arguments and evidence
points.brief: Arguments are the reasons that support a contention, backed by evidence such as statistics, expert views and examples.

points.title: Sequence and structure of an argument
points.brief: The order of arguments, from an opening anecdote to a final call to action, guides readers to the writer's view.

points.title: Persuasive techniques
points.brief: Writers persuade with techniques such as appeals to emotion or fairness, inclusive language, rhetorical questions and attacks on opponents.

points.title: Tone and its effect
points.brief: A writer's tone, such as outraged, measured or sarcastic, shapes how readers feel about the issue and the writer.

points.title: Visuals in persuasive texts
points.brief: Cartoons, photos and graphics can persuade by mocking, shocking or supporting the written argument.

chapters.title: Spoken argument and point of view

points.title: Persuasion in spoken texts
points.brief: In speeches, podcasts and videos, intonation, volume, pace, pauses and stress add to the persuasive effect of the words.

points.title: Context and argument
points.brief: When, where and for whom an argument appears changes how it is made and how audiences react.

points.title: Evaluating arguments
points.brief: Listening closely and asking questions shows when an argument is weak, such as generalising from one case or attacking a person instead of the idea.

points.title: Presenting your own point of view
points.brief: Students plan and present their own spoken point of view, choosing arguments and techniques that suit their audience.
